what: An API client is the one small wrapper around fetch that every request in your app goes through. It adds the shared rules: auth headers, timeouts, cancelling stale requests, and safe retries with backoff.
like: Like one front desk at a school office: every request goes through it, it knows the forms to fill, how long to wait, and when it is worth trying again.
why: One place to change auth, headers and error handling for the whole app
Cancelled and timed-out requests stop wasting bandwidth and never overwrite newer data
Retries recover from short blips without hammering a struggling server

steps.d: A component asks for data. The query cache answers from memory if the key is fresh; otherwise it calls the API client.
The client adds auth headers, base URL and a signal made with AbortSignal.any: one signal for the user or route cancelling, one for AbortSignal.timeout(ms).
The server answers. Network errors, 429 and 503 are transient; 400, 401, 403 and 404 are not and should fail at once.
Wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on with random jitter added, capped, and honour a Retry-After header if the server sends one.
When the user types again or leaves the page, abort the old request so a slow answer can never overwrite a newer one.

numbers.l: default retries for a failed query in TanStack Query (0 on the server)
cap on its default retry delay, which starts at 1 s and doubles each attempt
extra database load when 5 layers each retry 3 times (3 to the power 5), which is why you retry at one layer

choices.d: Retries multiply across layers. Pick one place, the client wrapper or the server-state library, and turn the others off.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them is safe. POST is not, so retry it only with an Idempotency-Key header, which is still an IETF draft.
AbortSignal.timeout(ms) gives a TimeoutError; AbortSignal.any([userSignal, timeoutSignal]) aborts on whichever comes first. Both are Baseline since 2024.
A thin fetch wrapper (or ky, axios) is enough for transport rules. For reads, let TanStack Query own retry, dedupe and cancellation per query key.

instead.why: For reads it already retries, dedupes and cancels per query key, so you write less transport code
When a dependency is down, stop retrying and fail fast instead of backing off forever

breaks.d: After an outage every client retries on the same schedule.
breaks.see: A traffic spike right after recovery and repeated 429s
breaks.fix: Exponential backoff with jitter, a small attempt cap, and honour Retry-After

breaks.d: A POST times out but the first one actually succeeded, then gets retried.
breaks.fix: Send an Idempotency-Key per user action, or do not auto-retry non-idempotent calls

breaks.d: A slow older request finishes after a newer one.
breaks.see: Search results jump back to an old query
breaks.fix: Abort the previous request with its AbortController and ignore the AbortError

say: Every call goes through one fetch wrapper that adds auth, a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout, and a cancel signal combined with AbortSignal.any.
I retry only transient failures - network errors, 429 and 503 - with exponential backoff, jitter and a cap, honouring Retry-After, and only at one layer.
POSTs are retried only with an idempotency key, and I abort superseded requests so stale data cannot win.

followups.a: Without it, all clients that failed together retry together and re-create the spike. Random spread breaks the synchronisation.

followups.q: How do you tell a timeout from a user cancel?
followups.a: AbortSignal.timeout aborts with a TimeoutError, while a manual abort() gives an AbortError, so the catch block can branch on err.name.
Client errors such as 400 or 404 will fail the same way again, and non-idempotent calls can cause duplicate side effects.

today: AbortSignal.timeout() and AbortSignal.any() are now Baseline in every major browser, so a small fetch wrapper handles timeouts and cancellation natively, while server-state libraries such as TanStack Query supply retry, backoff and dedupe per query.

check.q: A fetch with AbortSignal.timeout(5000) hits the limit. What is err.name?
check.why: A timeout abort uses a TimeoutError; AbortError is for a manual abort or user action.

check.q: Which call is NOT safe to retry automatically?
check.why: POST can create duplicates. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent.

check.q: Five layers each retry 3 times. The database could see how much extra load?
check.why: Retries multiply across layers, so retry at one place only.
